h1: Learning data skills as a working brewer
title: Learning Data Skills as a Working Brewer | Craft Beer School
desc: How a working brewer can learn useful data skills step by step, from clean logs and control charts to dashboards and Python.
teaser: Your brewery already collects data. Most of it sits in a notebook nobody reads. Here is how to make it useful.
standfirst: Brewers measure gravity, temperature, pH and volume every day. Very few use those numbers to find patterns. Data skills turn that habit into decisions. You can learn them alongside a brewing job. Here is a practical order to learn them in.
sections:
Every brew generates numbers: malt weights, mash temperatures, run-off times, original gravity, fermentation readings, final gravity, volumes and losses. Quality checks add pH, colour, bitterness and dissolved oxygen. A small brewpub can easily generate thousands of data points a year.

Most of it ends up in a logbook or a spreadsheet nobody revisits. The brewer who learns to look at it across batches starts to see things others miss: an efficiency that drops every monsoon, a yeast that slows after its fourth generation, a beer whose losses are twice the others.

Data skills start before any analysis. If your logs use different units, different names for the same beer or gaps where readings were skipped, no tool will fix them. Begin with one table per process, one row per brew or reading and the same columns every time.

Our guide to spreadsheet skills for logs and costing covers this foundation. It is not glamorous. It is where most brewery data projects fail.

The most useful idea in brewery data is variation. Every process wobbles a little. The question is whether a change is normal wobble or a real shift. Statistical process control (SPC) answers that question with a simple chart.

Plot a measurement in time order, such as original gravity for each batch of your core beer. Calculate the average and the standard deviation. Draw control limits at the average plus and minus three standard deviations. Points inside the limits are normal variation. A point outside, or a run of seven or more points on one side of the average, suggests something has changed and is worth investigating.

This one chart, kept up to date, catches drift in brewhouse efficiency, fermentation time or bitterness long before a customer notices.

Start with one beer and one measurement. Twenty batches give you enough points to draw sensible limits. Recalculate them only when you deliberately change the process, such as a new mill gap or a new malt supplier, not every time a point looks awkward.

Once records are clean, a dashboard puts the key numbers in one place. Tools such as Power BI, Tableau or Looker Studio connect to a spreadsheet and refresh automatically. A good brewery dashboard is small: volume brewed, efficiency, losses, fermentation times and quality results, each with a target.

The test of a dashboard is whether someone changes what they do because of it. If the head brewer looks at it on Monday and decides which tank to clean first, it works. If nobody opens it, it is decoration.
Step four: Python, if you want to go further

Python with the pandas library handles data too big or messy for a spreadsheet. It can merge logs from different systems, clean them automatically and produce charts in a few lines of code. Free tools such as Jupyter notebooks make it easy to experiment.

You do not need Python to get value from brewery data. Many brewers never go beyond spreadsheets and dashboards. That is fine. But if you enjoy it, Python opens the door to forecasting, predicting fermentation finish times and using sensor data from tanks.
Brewing knowledge is the hard part

Data tools are easy to learn compared with brewing. Anyone can draw a control chart. Knowing that a drop in attenuation might come from a mash temperature probe that has drifted half a degree, or from tired yeast, or from a new malt lot, takes brewing knowledge. That is why brewers who learn data skills are more useful than data analysts who learn about beer.

Our profile of a Master Brewer who works in data and AI shows where the two skills can lead together. It is a combination the industry is short of.

• Month one: clean up one process log and keep it consistent.
  • Month two: build a control chart for one key measurement and update it every batch.
  • Month three: make a one page dashboard for your head brewer.
  • After that: learn basic Python if you want to go further.

Your first step: pick one number your brewery measures on every batch, such as original gravity for your best seller, collect the last 20 values and plot them in order. Look at the spread and ask what caused the highest and lowest values.
faqs: What data skills does a brewer need?
Clean record keeping, basic spreadsheet analysis and control charts cover most needs. Dashboards and Python are useful next steps for those who want to go further.
What is a control chart in brewing?
It is a chart of a measurement in time order with an average and control limits, usually three standard deviations either side. Points outside the limits suggest the process has changed.
Do I need to learn Python?
No. Many brewers get most of the value from spreadsheets and dashboards. Python helps with larger or messier data sets and more advanced analysis.
